reviewer.summary: All nine planned claims are addressed, and the headline estimates, intervals and counts match the cited final findings. The report generally distinguishes local citation associations from causal or historical claims. Before release, qualify the eligibility sensitivity summary and narrow the description of the outgoing-link checks to what was actually verified.

issues.problem: “Including works that were never cited within the window but whose references were cited, and whose disruption score is therefore zero, gives nearly the same results.” This glosses over a change in the review–article comparison: its 95% interval narrowly excludes zero under the broader eligibility rule but not under the main rule. The short-window slope also changes from −2.82 to −4.03 points per doubling on the respective eligible samples (F17, F18).
issues.fix: Replace with: “Including works whose references were cited but that were not themselves cited preserves the main conclusions, but some estimates change. The review–article slope contrast narrowly excludes zero only under the broader rule, and the estimated short-window decline is steeper under that rule.” Cite F17 and F18 alongside T87.

issues.problem: “Where counts required listing citing works directly, repeated identifiers were removed and outgoing links were checked for citations to the work and its references.” This implies that outgoing links were checked for every directly retrieved citing work. T27 records reference-overlap classification for focal-citation streams; T24 documents a separate outbound-link check on 122 records from one residual stream.
issues.fix: Replace with: “Directly retrieved lists were deduplicated and checked against expected counts. For lists of works citing the focal work, outgoing links were used to classify whether each citing work also cited a reference. A separate check verified reference membership and exclusion from earlier portions for 122 records in one residual stream.” Cite T24, T26 and T27.

issues.problem: “Verdict: the full claim did not reproduce as stated.” The explanation is sound, but the label is less precise than F13: one part reproduced and the other parts were inconclusive, not contradicted.
issues.fix: Use “Partly reproduced: the decline was clear in the least-cited half, but not established in the middle or top groups, and the evidence did not establish a steeper decline at the top.” Use the same status in the verdict table.

issues.problem: “For works cited during the two full calendar years after publication, we asked what share of those citations came in the first of those years.” This can be read as pooling citations across works, whereas the reported contrast averages shares calculated separately for each work.
issues.fix: Say that, among works cited at least once across the two full calendar years, the team calculated each work’s first-year share and then compared the design-weighted group averages (F16, T78).

issues.problem: “Holding the works fixed kept a work from dropping out of the comparison just because it was not cited by the shorter cutoff.” Works with no citation by the shorter cutoff were in fact excluded from both sides of this comparison.
issues.fix: Replace with: “We restricted both estimates to works cited by the shorter cutoff, so the comparison did not mix a change in follow-up with a change in which works were included.”

reader.summary: The report’s main message is accessible, and the worked scoring example helps. But readers still have to reconstruct several key comparisons from captions and appendices. Define the sampling and ranking rules before using them, distinguish scores below zero from scores at or below zero, and explain what each comparison includes. The figures and tables will be easier to use once their labels name the quantities directly and the reference-model results say what the reported differences mean.

issues.problem: The title introduces “disruption and development,” and the summary says “Larger teams were more often on the developmental side of that measure.” A reader has not yet been told which citation pattern counts as development.
issues.fix: Use a plain title such as “How later research cites work by smaller and larger teams.” In the summary, say: “For larger teams, later works more often cited the new work together with at least one of its sources than cited it without any of its sources. The original study called this pattern development and the reverse pattern disruption.”

issues.problem: “The study’s finding that the full spread of disruption scores differs by team size reproduced in this sample” leaves both “the study” and “the full spread” unclear. “Its spread across research fields, the kinds of references used, and the timing of early citations” names topics without saying what the sample showed.
issues.fix: Say: “The mix of disruption scores differed by team size in our sample, as it did in the original study. Larger teams generally ranked lower on disruption, but not in every field or at every team size. They tended to cite newer and more highly cited sources. The largest teams also received a greater share of their early citations sooner than solo authors did.” Then say which parts of the original findings these observations do not establish.

issues.problem: In “The full claim about highly cited work did not reproduce as stated. The decline was clear in the least-cited half,” the reader has to infer what declined and what the original claim predicted. “What happened in the middle or at the top” does not name the groups.
issues.fix: Say: “The original study reported that disruption rank fell as teams grew, especially among the most-cited works. Here the decline was clear in the least-cited half. The evidence was too uncertain to tell whether ranks fell in the middle group or the most-cited tenth, or whether they fell faster in the most-cited tenth than in the least-cited half.”

issues.problem: “Recorded funding acknowledgments allow a narrower comparison, not a test of funding itself” does not say what is actually compared. “Open-source software projects” is not explained when the original study’s sources are introduced.
issues.fix: Say: “We could compare works with and without a funding acknowledgment in the index. That does not tell us whether the work actually received funding or what difference funding made.” On first use, describe open-source software projects as “software projects that make their code publicly available.”

issues.problem: “The sampling list required a usable recorded reference and some evidence of being cited” is too vague to distinguish entry into the sampling list from entry into the analysis. The appendix’s rule, “It excluded 10,720 with no recorded reference link and a recorded reference count of zero,” also leaves open what happened when the index recorded a positive reference count but supplied no link.
issues.fix: State the two rules separately. Explain exactly what reference information put a work on the sampling list and what was necessary to calculate its score. In the appendix, say: “We excluded 10,720 works for which the index listed no reference links and reported a reference count of zero.” Then state explicitly whether records with a positive count but no usable link could enter the list or the analysis. For the main analysis, say that a distinct later work had to cite the sampled work itself by the cutoff.

issues.problem: “Byline positions for which the index did not resolve a person’s identity” and “works less likely to be drawn count more” are harder than necessary. The latter does not yet explain what a weight is.
issues.fix: Say: “We counted every listed author position, even when OpenAlex could not identify the person. We sampled separately by team size so that large teams would be represented. In calculating results, we gave each sampled work more influence if it represented more works on the sampling list. We call this its sampling weight.”

issues.problem: “The sign tells us which of the first two citation patterns is more common” and “smaller in magnitude without changing its sign” make the reader translate mathematical language and do not explain a tie.
issues.fix: After the worked example, say: “A positive score means more later works cited the paper without any of its references than cited both. A negative score means the reverse. If those counts are equal, the score is zero. Citations to the references alone move a nonzero score closer to zero without changing which pattern is more common.”

issues.problem: “A raw score tells us about the balance of citation patterns for a work. A percentile rank tells us where the score stands relative to other eligible works published in the same year. Ties share a rank.” The reader has to wait until Figure 1 and the appendix to learn what the rank scale is and that sampling weights affect rank as well as the plotted averages.
issues.fix: Say: “The raw score is the number calculated above, before any comparison with other works. The percentile rank puts it on a scale from 0 to 100 among works from the same publication year that qualify for that analysis. Higher ranks mean higher scores. Works with the same score share a rank. Works that were less likely to be sampled count more when we calculate ranks as well as averages.”

issues.problem: “Including works that were never cited within the window but whose references were cited, and whose disruption score is therefore zero, gives nearly the same results” packs together the alternative inclusion rule, the reason for the score, and the outcome. “Nearly the same” also hides an exception visible in the article and review comparison.
issues.fix: Say: “We also repeated the analysis after admitting sampled works whose references received citations during the window even though the works themselves did not. These works score zero because neither of the first two citation patterns occurred. The main team-size result changed little. The appendix shows which comparisons changed, including the difference between the estimates for reviews and articles.”

issues.problem: “Most ranges are 95% confidence intervals from a bootstrap” names the interval without saying how it was taken from the repeated estimates. “The comparisons within authors use intervals that also account for repeated appearances of authors and works” can sound as if those are the same bootstrap intervals with an extra step.
issues.fix: Say: “For most results, we repeatedly drew a new sample from the works in each team-size group, allowing the same work to be drawn more than once. This is called a bootstrap. We report the middle 95% of the resulting estimates as the confidence interval. An interval for one point does not give an interval for the entire curve or for a difference between points.” Describe the method for the within-author intervals separately and say whether it uses the same repeated draws.

issues.problem: “A doubling of team size was associated with a decline of 3.48 percentile points in disruption rank” is the headline result, but the report does not explain until the appendix how one number summarizes the many team sizes. “Think of that estimate as a summary of comparisons such as two authors versus four” leaves open whether actual pairs were compared.
issues.fix: Say: “We fitted a trend across works with one to ten authors. We fitted it so that each doubling, such as going from two authors to four, corresponds to the same estimated change. The fitted decline was 3.48 points on the disruption rank scale for each doubling. The 95% interval ranged from a decline of 2.70 to 4.27 points, based on 6,210 works. Individual team sizes did not always follow this trend.”

issues.problem: Several results sections open with background rather than the result: “The original study found a steady decline in disruption rank and a rise in typical citation counts as teams grew”; “The original study reported declines across fields and subfields and within most journals”; and “The original study reported that larger teams drew on newer and more popular sources.”
issues.fix: Lead with what this sample showed: “Larger teams generally ranked lower on disruption but received more citations”; “The decline appeared in most fields with enough data, but not in all of them”; and “In the team sizes shown, larger teams cited newer and generally more highly cited sources.” Follow each with the original finding, retaining details such as the comparison up to 100 contributors.

issues.problem: “Their respective 95% intervals were 3 to 4, 13 to 17, and 31 to 46, based on 600, 624 and 477 works” makes the reader match three lists. “The largest group” is not named until the caption.
issues.fix: Keep each result together: “For 600 solo works, the median was 4 citing works, with a 95% interval of 3 to 4. For 624 works with ten authors, it was 15, with an interval of 13 to 17. For 477 works with 51 to 100 authors, it was 39, with an interval of 31 to 46.”

issues.problem: Figure 1 says “Panel A averages each work’s disruption percentile” without naming what each plotted point averages over. “The counts below the equally spaced team sizes are the actual numbers of works” and “reversals and plateaus” also require the reader to translate chart conventions.
issues.fix: Say: “In panel A, each point is the average disruption rank for one team size or size range. Along the horizontal axis, categories are evenly spaced even though some cover several team sizes. The number below each category is the number of sampled works, counted once each. The dotted line marks where the chart switches from individual sizes to ranges.” In the verdict, say that the measures sometimes level off or move in the opposite direction between neighbouring categories.

issues.problem: After directing the reader to look “just before zero,” the report says “the interval on the difference at zero accounts for the sampling design.” At zero the curve includes works that score exactly zero; the reported comparison excludes them. “Ten-author work was 29.4 percentage points more likely to score below zero than solo work” also sounds less direct than a difference in shares.
issues.fix: Say: “The share scoring below zero was 29.4 percentage points higher for works with ten authors than for solo works. The 95% interval was 24.0 to 34.5 points, based on 1,224 works. Read this difference just to the left of zero in Figure 2. It excludes works that scored exactly zero. This interval is for that one difference, not for the difference between the curves across their full range.” Apply the same correction to “estimated the difference at zero” in the summary table.

issues.problem: Figure 2 says the horizontal axis “spreads out values near zero” but does not tell the reader how to read the spacing. “This is not a panel-for-panel redraw of the original study. Its closest comparison is the Extended Data analysis” describes the history or format of the figure rather than helping the reader use it.
issues.fix: Say: “The axis shows scores from negative 0.1 to positive 0.1. It gives more space to small differences near zero, so equal distances along the axis do not always represent equal changes in score.” Explain the tick marks if needed. End with “Compare with the analysis of score distributions by team size in the original study’s Extended Data.”

issues.problem: “Most scores were small in absolute terms. And ranking above larger teams does not imply that most solo work had positive scores” asks the reader to translate “absolute” and infer the practical distinction between score and rank.
issues.fix: Say: “Most scores were close to zero, whether positive or negative. Solo works tended to rank above works by larger teams, but only 44.3% of solo works had a positive score.”

issues.problem: The text uses “the least-cited half” and “the middle and highest citation groups” before defining their boundaries. Figure 3 says weighting applies “both when setting the groups from those ranks and when calculating the plotted averages,” which does not make clear why the lowest half need not contain half the sampled records.
issues.fix: Before giving the estimates, say: “Within each publication year, we ranked works by how many distinct later works cited them. The lower group was below the 50th percentile. The middle group began at the 50th and stopped just before the 90th. The top tenth began at the 90th. These boundaries use sampling weights, so the lower half of the weighted ranking need not contain half the sampled records. The legend counts each sampled record once.”

issues.problem: Figure 3 says “A work is more disruptive when later works cite it instead of citing it together with its references.” That can sound as if citing a work without its sources is the whole measure. “The ranges above ten authors are shown for comparison only” does not say what they were left out of.
issues.fix: Say: “Disruption scores compare citations to a work without any of its references with citations to the work and at least one reference. Citations to the references alone also count in the total used to scale the score. The figure plots all team-size groups, but the estimated change per doubling uses only works with one to ten authors.”

issues.problem: The text says “the vertical rank scale runs from 0 to 100, but the chart displays only part of that range” without naming the displayed limits. The caption also repeats the detailed estimates that the text introduces and the appendix tabulates.
issues.fix: Say: “Disruption ranks can run from 0 to 100. This chart shows only the part between [give the two displayed limits].” Keep the caption focused on what the points and bars show, where to look, and which sizes enter the trend. Put the detailed estimates and intervals together in the text or table rather than making the reader reconcile several versions.

issues.problem: “The estimate points away from a steeper decline at the top, but is uncertain” requires the reader to work out why a higher estimated change means a less steep decline.
issues.fix: Say: “The best estimate suggests a weaker decline in the most-cited tenth, not a stronger one. But the interval allows both a stronger and a weaker decline than in the least-cited half, so the data do not settle the comparison.”

issues.problem: “We kept groups only if they had enough works and a range of team sizes” leaves the method in the Figure 4 caption. In that caption, “at least 5 in each of the 1–2 and 5–10 author ranges” leaves the reader to supply both what is counted and how the rules apply.
issues.fix: Say in the methods for this comparison: “We estimated the trend using works with one to ten authors. To qualify, a field, subfield or journal needed at least 30 works, including at least 5 with one or two authors and at least 5 with five to ten authors. It also needed at least 4 distinct team sizes.” Explain that OpenAlex assigns a broad subject and a narrower subject within it.

issues.problem: “The estimates lean negative rather than pointing in one direction everywhere” and Figure 4’s “Many field intervals include zero” do not explain as directly as they could what is and is not established. The figure title, “Disruption rank by team size in fields with enough data,” does not signal the accompanying subfield and journal table.
issues.fix: Say: “In most eligible fields and subfields, the best estimate was a decline. In many individual fields, the interval still allowed no change or an increase.” Use a title such as “How disruption ranks change with team size across research fields.” In the caption, say that the dots show individual fields and that the table summarizes how many fields, subfields and journals qualified and how many had estimated declines.

issues.problem: “The second table column counts groups that met those requirements out of all groups seen in the sample” and “keeps the same groups in each draw” make the reader work out the denominator and what is held fixed.
issues.fix: Say: “The second column shows how many groups qualified out of all groups represented in the sample. Each qualifying field, subfield or journal counts once in its own comparison, regardless of how many works it contains. We use the same list of qualifying groups for each repeat draw.”

issues.problem: “When we first averaged references within each work instead” does not identify what was averaged. In Figure 5, “Each link carries that work’s weight” introduces “link” in a different sense from an ordinary web link and makes the two kinds of weighting hard to separate.
issues.fix: Say: “In Figure 5, each reference counts once for each sampled work that lists it. It receives that work’s sampling weight. This gives longer reference lists more influence. For a separate comparison, we calculated the average age of each work’s references first, so a long list did not give that work more influence. On that basis, references in ten-author works were 5.20 years newer on average, with a 95% interval of 4.41 to 6.05 years, across 1,221 works.”

issues.problem: Figure 5 says “Reference age is the difference in publication years” without giving the direction of subtraction. “Its scale is linear through one citation and logarithmic above one” is not explained until a separate “Reading Figure 5” paragraph. “Current citation totals, not totals at publication” could refer to the publication of either work.
issues.fix: Put the explanations in the caption: “Reference age is how many calendar years earlier the reference appeared than the work listing it. In panel B, the axis uses ordinary spacing up to one citation. Above one citation, equal steps mean multiplying the count by ten. Panel B uses the citation totals available when the data were collected, not the totals when the work listing each reference was published.” Give the collection date if known.

issues.problem: “Very highly cited references follow the pattern the original study proposed,” “neither model fits closely,” and “the comparison of the fitted shapes among highly cited references was inconclusive” leave the reader without a clear account of what the models assume or how their fit was judged. The caption, reading note and verdict repeat the result without resolving this.
issues.fix: Separate the observed result from the model checks. Say: “The figure compares the reference lists directly. Separately, we tested a model in which the share of references older than a cutoff falls by the same fraction for each extra year of age. We also tested a model in which very high citation counts get rarer in a particular mathematical pattern, using references with at least 50 citations.” Explain how closely the predicted shares matched the observed shares and what a difference between the teams would mean. Keep the model explanation and result in one place.

issues.problem: “For works cited during the two full calendar years after publication, we asked what share of those citations came in the first of those years” can be read as requiring citations in both years. “Another check asked how much early attention arrived in the publication year itself” does not give that measure’s denominator until the appendix.
issues.fix: Define both shares together: “For the first comparison, we counted citations in the first and second full calendar years after publication and asked what share came in the first. A work needed at least one citation in either year. For the second comparison, we counted citations from publication through the end of the second full calendar year and asked what share came in the publication year itself.”

issues.problem: “The comparison put the groups on the same footing by publication year and quarter” does not say what was done. “The score and the timing measures also share some of the same citations” does not explain why that matters.
issues.fix: Say: “We compared the groups as if they had the same mix of publication years and three-month periods within each year. This matters because works published late in the year have less time to receive a citation that year. Some citations enter both the disruption score and the timing measure, so the two measures are not independent evidence.”

issues.problem: “We focused on identified Columbia authors who had works with different team sizes. A regression summarizes the association with team size while allowing the average rank to differ by year, topic and author.” This leaves the reader unsure which works entered, what made this a comparison within authors, and what adjustment changed.
issues.fix: Say: “We used works by authors whom OpenAlex identified and linked to Columbia and who appeared on works with different numbers of authors. We fitted a trend across those works. The fitted comparison lets each author, publication year and topic have a different average rank, rather than counting those differences as part of the team-size pattern. We also fitted a simpler trend to exactly the same works. That lets us compare the two methods without changing which works are included.” State the team-size limits used in this analysis.

issues.problem: “OpenAlex articles showed a decline, but the review estimate was too uncertain to establish one. The main comparison between their slopes was also inconclusive” uses an unexplained database category and “slopes” before the appendix defines the term. “Theoretical from empirical work” is not explained on first use.
issues.fix: Say: “Under the main citation rule, works that OpenAlex classified as articles ranked lower as team size increased. For works classified as reviews, the evidence did not establish a decline. A direct comparison did not clearly establish that the two groups differed in how much rank changed per doubling. The index did not reliably distinguish work that develops or studies theories from work based on observations or experiments.”

issues.problem: “Holding the works fixed kept a work from dropping out of the comparison just because it was not cited by the shorter cutoff” sounds as though works not cited by the short cutoff were kept. “Each window uses all its own eligible works” does not identify the alternative sets.
issues.fix: Say: “For the direct comparison, we used only works that met the citation requirement in both windows. This let us change the cutoff without changing the set of works. We calculated ranks separately for each window on that same set. The appendix also gives estimates that use every work meeting the rule for each window on its own.”

issues.problem: “The estimated decline was clearer for works with no acknowledgment on record” invites a comparison based on two separate intervals. “The appendix reports the direct contrast” sends the reader elsewhere for the estimate that answers whether the groups differ.
issues.fix: Keep the separate estimates and add the direct comparison in the text: “The estimated change in disruption rank per doubling of team size was 4.26 points higher for works with an acknowledgment on record than for works without one. The 95% interval was 2.68 to 5.83 points higher, based on 6,210 works. This is a difference between record categories, not an estimate of what funding does.”

issues.problem: The overview table uses shorthand that is harder to read than the results: “Reproduced locally,” “Model parameters varied with team size,” “the age-model comparison agreed in direction,” “after adjustment,” and “other score variants.”
issues.fix: Use wording the reader can lift directly from the results: “We found the same difference in this sample”; “The original study reported that the rate at which older references became rarer, and the shape of the highest citation counts, differed by team size”; “Older references became rarer faster with age in ten-author work than in solo work, as in the original study”; “after comparing works by the same authors and allowing for differences by year and topic”; and “other ways of calculating the score.”

issues.problem: “Works who found an audience only years later,” “one university-linked cohort,” “too few mixed-size teams in most journals,” and “verified funding histories” obscure otherwise straightforward limitations.
issues.fix: Say: “We cannot identify works that received little attention at first but were cited much later. This sample of works linked to one university cannot stand in for the original collections. Most journals had too few works across the required range of team sizes. We could not verify which works actually received funding.”

issues.problem: “The screen matters for whom the results describe,” “cohorts with different amounts of follow-up,” and “dependencies from shared citations across works” are dense. “A date cutoff is not a historical copy of the citation index” makes the reader infer what the date does and does not establish.
issues.fix: Say: “The sample rules limit which works these results describe. Ranking works within a publication year avoids comparing works from years that had different amounts of time to collect citations. But even within a year, works published earlier had more time.” Then say: “The cutoff uses publication dates. It does not tell us what records the index contained on that date. The intervals do not account for index errors, the same later publication affecting the scores of several works, or differences at other universities.”

issues.problem: “Evidence meant a positive lifetime count in the local copy of OpenAlex, a positive count for a later calendar year through the cutoff year, or a strictly later citing work found in the local records.” A reader has to decode three checks, the two meanings of “local,” and the difference between a year-level count and the exact citation window.
issues.fix: Say: “To enter the sampling list, a work had to pass at least one of three checks. Our copy of OpenAlex either reported at least one citation in total, reported at least one citation in a calendar year after publication and no later than the cutoff year, or contained a citing work with a publication date after the sampled work’s date. Passing one of these checks did not prove that a citation fell within the exact dates used in the main analysis.”

issues.problem: “The local list contained 55,371 works” does not name the list. In “Among the reference exclusions, 3,507 had a positive lifetime count, 3,188 had a later-year citation count, and 482 had a dated local citing work; these categories can overlap,” the significance of the overlap is buried.
issues.fix: Say: “Before applying the reference and citation requirements, the list contained 55,371 Columbia-linked works. Some works excluded for lack of references still had evidence of being cited. Among them, 3,507 had at least one citation reported in total, 3,188 had a citation reported in a later calendar year, and 482 had a dated later citing work in our copy of the index. A work could count in more than one of these groups.”

issues.problem: “Drawn at random without replacement within each team-size group, from sorted OpenAlex work identifiers, using the PCG64 random number generator with seed 42” packs the design and the reproducibility settings into one sentence. “The original weights stayed in place after the window-specific eligibility checks, and no ineligible draw was replaced” uses unnecessary process shorthand.
issues.fix: Say: “We drew works at random from each team-size group. No work could be drawn twice. To make the draw repeatable, we sorted the records by their OpenAlex identifying numbers and used the PCG64 random-number method with 42 as its starting value. If a work failed the citation rule for a window, we did not replace it. The remaining works kept the weights from the initial draw.”

issues.problem: “In the years with complete short follow-up, 5,966 works qualified for the main-window analysis; the 5,671 cited in the shorter window also qualified in the main window. When citations to references alone were allowed, 7,997 works qualified in the main window and 6,010 in the shorter window and in the comparison using the same works in both windows.” The populations and the reason the last two counts match are difficult to untangle.
issues.fix: Say: “Among works with enough time for the shorter window, 5,966 met the rule for the main window. Of those, 5,671 also met the rule for the shorter window. When we also admitted works whose references alone were cited, 7,997 qualified for the main window and 6,010 qualified for the shorter window. Those same 6,010 qualified in both windows, so we used them for the direct comparison under that rule.” Point out that these counts cover all sampled team sizes, unlike the trend estimates restricted to one to ten authors.

issues.problem: “Dates and distinct reference lists came from the local copy of OpenAlex. Later citing works came from the global index.” The scope of each source is unclear. “Assigning a citing work to only one part,” “repeated identifiers,” and “outgoing links” do not explain how double counting was avoided.
issues.fix: Say: “We took publication dates and lists of references from our copy of OpenAlex. We looked for later citing works throughout OpenAlex, not just among works linked to Columbia. A later work could cite references in more than one part of a long list. We counted it only in the first part it matched. When we retrieved individual citing records, we removed duplicates and checked the citing works’ own reference lists for the sampled work and its sources.”

issues.problem: “All 62 comparisons between grouped totals and independently checked totals agreed,” “the remaining portion of a long reference list,” “seven checked work-year comparisons,” and “complete against their expected counts” leave the objects of the checks implicit.
issues.fix: Say: “In all 62 checks, the totals calculated by grouping records matched the totals calculated separately. All 122 citing works checked in a later part of a long reference list cited a reference in that part and none in an earlier part. In seven checks for individual works and years, reversing the order of the parts did not change the totals. Each of the 79 lists retrieved directly contained the expected number of distinct citing works.”

issues.problem: “The weighted percentile is the percentage of weight below a value plus half the weight tied at that value, as a share of all eligible weight” mixes a percentage with quantities that have not yet been divided by the total. “A weighted regression against the base-two logarithm of team size expresses the slope as the expected difference” introduces three technical terms at once.
issues.fix: Say: “For works from the same year that qualify for an analysis, add the sampling weights of works with a lower value and half the weights of works with the same value. Divide by the total weight and express the result as a percentage. For example, if weights total 100, with 40 below a score and 20 tied, the rank is 50.” Then say: “The regression fits a trend that gives works their sampling weights. It uses a team-size scale on which each doubling is one step: two to four authors is the same step as four to eight. The slope is the fitted change in rank for one such step.”

issues.problem: “We resampled the largest group too, even though every work on the sampling list was selected for it; there was no reduction in estimated uncertainty for having sampled the entire group” states the choice but leaves a reader unsure what the interval for that group represents.
issues.fix: Say: “We treated the largest team-size group the same as the other groups in the 1,000 repeat draws, even though we selected all 481 of its works from the sampling list. The intervals therefore do not get narrower to reflect that full coverage.” Explain what kind of variation the interval is intended to describe; it is not uncertainty about which of the 481 listed works were selected.

issues.problem: “For the regressions with author comparisons, each work’s weight was split among its qualifying authors. Those regressions kept the ranks fixed and accounted for repeated appearances by the same author and by the same work. The main author comparison used 1,885 authors, with 6,838 author–work entries across 4,107 unique works.” The unit of analysis and the relationship between the two uncertainty methods remain hard to follow.
issues.fix: Say: “A work could enter the within-author comparison once for each author who qualified. We divided its sampling weight among those authors so the work did not gain weight from appearing more than once. The comparison covered 1,885 authors and 4,107 distinct works, giving 6,838 records pairing an author with a work. The interval calculation did not recalculate ranks and allowed records sharing an author or a work to be related.” Name and briefly explain the interval method, and distinguish it from the separate bootstrap interval for the unadjusted trend.

issues.problem: “There were 446,323 distinct work–reference pairs in the main reference comparison, involving 373,977 unique references” and “The 10,732 same-year pairs remain” introduce database language where a counting example would be clearer.
issues.fix: Say: “We counted a reference once for each sampled work that listed it. That gave 446,323 records covering 373,977 different references. We omitted a record from the age calculation if its reference had no publication year or appeared later than the sampled work. We kept the 10,732 records where the sampled work and the reference appeared in the same year.” Keep the separate missing-year, later-year and missing-count totals with their respective rules.

issues.problem: “We add one to each reference's citation total before taking its base-two logarithm, so very highly cited references do not dominate the averages” gives examples of calculations but not how to interpret the differences in the table. The figure and table also use different scales.
issues.fix: Say: “For the averages in the table, we first add one to the citation count. We then use a scale that goes up by one each time that adjusted count doubles. For example, one citation becomes one and three citations become two. This reduces the influence of very highly cited references. A difference in this table is a difference between averages on that scale, not a difference in numbers of citations. Figure 5 plots the citation counts themselves.”

issues.problem: “A geometric model for reference age, the whole-year version of an exponential decline,” “a discrete power law,” “count raised to a fixed negative power,” and the table labels “Difference in fitted age decay” and “Difference in fitted citation exponent” do not tell a neighbouring researcher what the reported differences measure.
issues.fix: Say: “The age model assumes that the share of references older than a cutoff falls by the same fraction for each additional year. The citation model applies to whole-number citation counts of at least 50 and describes how quickly references become rarer as their citation counts rise.” Define the exact quantities subtracted in the two table rows, including what a positive difference means. Give a short worked example so the reader can interpret the values rather than just recognize the model names.

issues.problem: “The largest absolute gaps were about 0.081 for age, across 624 works and 34,531 pairs, and 0.088 for citation counts, across 620 works and 26,259 pairs in the fitted range” uses decimals without saying what a gap looks like in the data. “These gaps are descriptive, not tests treating references as independent observations” is hard to parse.
issues.fix: Say: “At the cutoff where the age model differed most from the observations, the shares differed by about 0.081, or 8.1 percentage points. This comparison used 34,531 reference records from 624 works. For citation counts, the largest gap was 0.088, or 8.8 percentage points, using 26,259 records from 620 works in the fitted range. These figures describe the mismatch. They are not results from a statistical test that treats each reference record as independent.”

issues.problem: “Each cell gives the estimate, its 95% interval in parentheses and the actual number of works. The two columns apply the two eligibility rules in each citation window.” This does not tell the reader how to parse the semicolon, what counts once, or how to read the reference table’s third results column. “Slopes and differences between slopes are percentile points for a doubling of team size” is not enough to decode abbreviated row labels.
issues.fix: Give a key: “The first number is the estimate; the parentheses give its 95% confidence interval. The number after the semicolon counts sampled works once each, without weighting. The first results column requires a citation to the work itself. The second also admits a work if only its references were cited. Both rules use the window named in the row, or the main window if none is named. The reference table adds a column with no citation requirement. In trend rows, a negative value means a lower disruption rank for a doubling of team size, unless the row gives a different unit.”

issues.problem: Several appendix labels are hard to scan: “Rank slope, one to ten authors,” “Mean rank, 51–100 minus ten,” “Fields with negative slopes (%),” and “Slope, reviews minus articles.”
issues.fix: Use “Change in disruption rank per doubling, teams with one to ten authors”; “Average disruption rank: teams with 51 to 100 authors compared with ten authors”; “Percentage of eligible fields with an estimated decline”; and “Difference in change per doubling: reviews compared with articles.” Apply the same pattern to the other team-size, citation-group and funding rows, making the direction of each subtraction explicit.

issues.problem: “The largest gap between the curves compares the share of work at or below each raw score. This is a weighted distance between the distributions” does not say what is maximized. “Largest gap between curves, ten versus solo (share)” is especially easy to confuse with the preceding difference in negative-score shares because some point estimates happen to match.
issues.fix: Say: “At each possible score, we calculated the weighted share of ten-author works at or below it and the corresponding share of solo works. We took the largest difference between those shares anywhere on the scale, regardless of which was higher. That is a different calculation from comparing only the share with scores below zero.” Give both rows plainly named units and explain that 0.294 as a share is 29.4 percentage points.

issues.problem: “Reference age, pooled (years),” “Reference citations, work averages (log scale),” “Links with usable age (%),” and “All sampled works” require the reader to look elsewhere for the counting rule and to work out why not all sampled works appear in every row.
issues.fix: Use “Difference in reference age, counting every listed reference (years),” “Difference in average reference citations per work, on the scale described above,” and “Percentage of reference records with enough date information to calculate age.” Label the last column “No citation requirement” and explain that each estimate still requires the reference information needed for that row.

issues.problem: “First full year, 51–100 minus solo” and “Publication year, negative minus positive score” give the numerators and groups but not the shares being compared. “Both eligibility rules give the same contrasts below because the shares require the work to be cited during the years compared” takes effort to connect back to the headings.
issues.fix: Define the two shares immediately above the table. Then write row labels such as “Share in the first full year: teams with 51 to 100 authors compared with solo works” and “Share in the publication year: works with negative scores compared with works with positive scores.” Say: “The two columns match because neither timing measure can be calculated for works that were not themselves cited in the period being compared.”

reviewer.summary: All nine planned claims receive a verdict and a reason. The headline estimates and intervals match the final-stage findings, and the report makes clear that the associations are local and noncausal. Before release, correct the timing estimate’s wording and label which works the appendix reference counts describe.

issues.problem: The sentence “The first full year accounted for 5.23 percentage points more of the early citation total for teams with 51 to 100 authors than for solo works” reads as a comparison of pooled citation totals. F16 and T78 estimate a difference between weighted averages of per-work shares. Those are different quantities.
issues.fix: Replace it with: “Among works with complete follow-up and at least one citation in the first two full calendar years, the weighted average share arriving in the first year was 5.23 percentage points higher for teams with 51 to 100 authors than for solo works.” Keep the reported interval and sample size.

issues.problem: The appendix says, “Counting a reference once per work that listed it gave 446,323 records covering 373,977 different references.” It does not identify the analysis subset. Those are the counts for works directly cited in the main window, not for all 8,000 sampled works. T3 and F10 give 448,173 pairs and 375,502 distinct references for the full sample.
issues.fix: Start the sentence with “Among works directly cited in the main window,” and state that the missing-year and missing-citation counts that follow use the same subset. If presenting a full-sample count as well, use the T3/F10 totals.

issues.problem: “The shorter-window decline was steeper under that rule” leaves the comparison implicit and can be read as an established difference between windows. Under the broader rule, the paired short-minus-main interval includes zero (F18).
issues.fix: Specify the comparison: “Under the broader eligibility rule, the short-window slope estimate was more negative than under the direct-citation rule (−4.03 versus −2.82 rank points per doubling). Within the broader sample, the paired difference between windows was inconclusive.”

issues.problem: “They examined research articles, US patents and software projects that make their code publicly available” adds a public-code eligibility condition not established by the paper brief.
issues.fix: Use “They examined research articles, US patents and GitHub software projects,” or cite a source that establishes the public-code condition.

reader.summary: The worked disruption example and the section headings give the report a clear structure. The main obstacles are distinguishing sampling from analysis eligibility, following the different uses of ranks and weights, and understanding what the uncertainty intervals compare. Several captions and appendix entries still depend on explanations elsewhere. Define those distinctions at first use and make each caption and table readable on its own.

issues.problem: “Larger teams also more often produced works that later publications cited together with at least one source rather than without any of their sources. Wu, Wang and Evans call the first citation pattern development and the reverse pattern disruption.” The reader has to work out whose sources these are and what “the reverse pattern” means.
issues.fix: Larger teams more often produced work that later publications cited alongside at least one reference from the work’s own reference list. Wu, Wang and Evans call citing a work alongside its references development. They call citing a work without any of its references disruption.

issues.problem: “The mix of disruption scores differed by team size, as it did in the original study.” The summary then says that larger teams “ranked lower on disruption.” Neither the score nor the distinction between a score and a rank is explained yet.
issues.fix: As in the original study, works by larger teams more often had scores below zero. That means more later publications cited the work alongside its references than cited it alone. Larger teams also generally ranked lower when we compared their scores with those of other works from the same year.

issues.problem: “The largest teams also received a greater share of their early citations sooner than solo authors did. The team-size pattern persisted when comparing work by the same authors and when using a shorter window or a simpler score.” A share cannot itself arrive sooner, and “the team-size pattern” could refer to several results in this paragraph.
issues.fix: A larger share of the biggest teams’ early citations arrived in the first full calendar year after publication than for solo works. Larger teams still tended to rank lower on disruption when we compared works by the same authors, counted citations over a shorter period, or used a simpler score.

issues.problem: “We did not establish the same pattern for reviews, a general rule for the citation counts of references, or what happens over long follow-up.” This combines three different questions, and “a general rule” does not say which result was inconclusive.
issues.fix: For reviews, we could not tell whether disruption rank fell with team size. We also could not tell whether very highly cited references became rarer at different rates for different team sizes. Our data did not track citations for long enough to test the original study’s findings over longer periods.

issues.problem: “The claim across citation levels did not reproduce as stated.” The opening makes readers wait for the next sentences to find out which claim failed.
issues.fix: We found a clear decline in disruption rank among the least-cited half of works. We could not establish the original study’s claim that the decline was steeper among the most-cited works.

issues.problem: “We could not test late recognition, historical growth in team size, patterns in corporate patents or the results for Nobel-winning work.” “Late recognition” and “Nobel-winning work” do not identify what would have been measured or compared.
issues.fix: We could not test whether work that drew little attention at first was cited much later, or whether teams grew over decades. We also lacked the data to repeat the original comparisons for company patents or research associated with Nobel Prizes.

issues.problem: “Each had at least one author who listed Columbia University or an institution that OpenAlex lists under it. The records cover several research outputs, not just journal articles. Team size counts every listed author position, even when OpenAlex could not identify the person.” The affiliation rule, the kinds of records included, and “author position” are underspecified for the reader.
issues.fix: We included a work if at least one author listed Columbia University or an institution that OpenAlex groups under Columbia. Name the kinds of research records included besides journal articles. We counted every entry in a work’s author list, even if OpenAlex could not match the entry to a person.

issues.problem: “We sampled separately by team size so that large teams would be represented. A sampled work has more influence in the calculations if it represents more works on the sampling list.” The main method does not say how the groups were formed or why a work represents more works. The appendix table ends at 100 authors, but the text does not explain how works with more than 100 authors were handled.
issues.fix: We drew works separately for each team size from one to ten authors and for teams of 11 to 20, 21 to 50, and 51 to 100 authors. State explicitly whether the sampling list excluded teams larger than 100 or contained none. A work counted for more if we drew a smaller fraction of its group. We call this its sampling weight.

issues.problem: “Getting on the sampling list was not the same as qualifying for the analysis. To enter the list, a work needed the identity of at least one distinct reference recorded in OpenAlex, other than the work itself. A reference count without a usable link was not enough. It also needed some evidence of being cited in our copy of the index, which could come from a total count, a count in a later calendar year or a dated citing work.” The paragraph makes the reader piece together the two eligibility rules and what an “identity” or “dated citing work” is.
issues.fix: The sampling list required a recorded link to at least one reference other than the work itself. A count of references did not qualify. The index also had to show some evidence that the work had been cited: a total citation count above zero, a count above zero in a later calendar year no later than the cutoff year, or a record of a citing publication dated after the work. The main analysis used a stricter rule: at least one identifiable later publication had to cite the work itself by the main cutoff.

issues.problem: “We need at least one citing work in these groups for the score to have meaning.” This can sound like the main eligibility rule, although a work can have a calculable score without itself being cited.
issues.fix: The calculation needs at least one later work in any of the three groups. If later works cite only the references, the score is zero. We left those cases out of the main analysis because it required a citation to the sampled work itself.

issues.problem: “The percentile rank puts it on a scale from 0 to 100 among eligible works from the same publication year. Higher ranks mean higher scores, and works with the same score share a rank.” This gives the scale but not what a number on it means. The relevant weights and treatment of ties are only fully explained in the appendix.
issues.fix: A percentile rank shows where a work’s score falls among eligible works published in the same year, on a scale from 0 to 100. It counts the weighted share with lower scores, plus half the weighted share with the same score. For example, if the weights total 100, with 40 below a score and 20 tied, the rank is 50.

issues.problem: “The shorter comparison ended on 31 December of the second calendar year after publication, not on the second anniversary.” It takes a moment to see that the shorter cutoff varies with the publication year, whereas the main cutoff does not.
issues.fix: The main count stopped on 23 November 2026 for every work. The shorter count stopped on 31 December of the second calendar year after each work was published. For a 2023 work, that was 31 December 2025. Works from 2024 were left out because their shorter period was not complete by the main cutoff.

issues.problem: “Including works cited only through their references, which therefore score zero, gives nearly the same main team-size result, though the review–article comparison and the short-window estimate change, as the appendix shows.” “Cited only through” sounds as though the work itself received a citation. The sentence also leaves the two changes unnamed.
issues.fix: We also checked what happened when we included works whose references were cited but that were not cited themselves. Those works score zero. The main team-size result changed little. The estimated decline over the shorter period was steeper, and the interval for the difference between reviews and articles just excluded no difference.

issues.problem: “An interval for a point is not an interval for the whole curve or for a difference between points. The regressions that compare work by the same authors use a different method, without repeated draws. Their intervals account for records that share an author or a work.” “Point” has not been tied to a plotted estimate, and “regressions” and the alternative uncertainty method are introduced without a plain explanation.
issues.fix: A bar or band shows the uncertainty for one plotted estimate at a time. It does not show the uncertainty for the whole curve or for the difference between two estimates. For the comparison of work by the same authors, we fitted a statistical trend, called a regression. Instead of drawing works again, we estimated uncertainty in a way that allows records involving the same author or the same work to be related.

issues.problem: “We fitted a trend across works with one to ten authors. The trend gives each doubling, such as going from two to four authors, the same estimated change.” “Gives” obscures that this is an assumption of the fitted trend, not a property of the observed data.
issues.fix: For works with one to ten authors, we fitted a line on a scale where doubling team size is one step. The line estimates the same change from two to four authors as from four to eight. The observed averages need not follow that line.

issues.problem: “Figure 1 puts average disruption ranks next to typical citation counts. Each point averages ranks, or shows the median citation count, for one team size or size range.” The reader has to sort out which points show which measure.
issues.fix: In Figure 1, panel A shows the average disruption rank for each team size or range. Panel B shows the median citation count for each group. The median is the middle count when works are put in order by how many citations they received.

issues.problem: “The counts below the equally spaced team sizes are the actual numbers of works. The dotted line separates individual sizes from size ranges.” This does not explain why equal spacing matters or how the counts differ from the weighted estimates.
issues.fix: Each team-size group takes up the same horizontal space, even when it covers several sizes. The numbers below the groups count each sampled work once. The dotted line marks where single team sizes end and ranges begin. Read the largest group as a whole, not as a result for each team size in it.

issues.problem: “A score is positive when more later works cite the work without citing any of its references than cite both the work and its references.” In Figure 2, “its references” can mean the whole list. Similarly, Figure 4 says “those that cite both” without saying how many references qualify.
issues.fix: A score is positive when more later works cite the sampled work without any of its references than cite it with at least one of its references. A negative score means the opposite. Use the same distinction in the other figure captions.

issues.problem: “The plot shows scores from negative 0.1 to positive 0.1 and spreads out values near zero.” Readers are not explicitly told that the display shows only part of the score range and that horizontal distances are not comparable across the plot.
issues.fix: The figure shows only the part of the score scale from negative 0.1 to positive 0.1. The horizontal axis gives more space to scores near zero, so equal distances can represent different changes in score.

issues.problem: “This is not a panel-for-panel redraw of the original study. Its closest comparison is the Extended Data analysis of differences in the full disruption-score distributions across team sizes.” The body then repeats the caveat and invokes “The brief,” which is not part of the reader’s account of the study.
issues.fix: In the caption only, say: Compare with the original study’s Extended Data analysis of how the full spread of scores differed by team size. There is no exact matching panel. Give the figure or panel number if it is known.

issues.problem: “The share scoring below zero was 29.4 percentage points higher for ten-author works than for solo works. The 95% interval was 24.0 to 34.5 points across 1,224 works. Read the difference just to the left of zero in Figure 2: it excludes exact zeros.” “Percentage points” is left unexplained, and “across” leaves the sample count’s role implicit.
issues.fix: In Figure 2, compare the curves just to the left of zero so that works scoring exactly zero are left out. The two shares were 77.6% for ten-author works and 48.2% for solo works. Subtracting them gives a difference of 29.4 percentage points. The comparison used 1,224 works and had a 95% interval of 24.0 to 34.5 percentage points.

issues.problem: “The lowest group was below the 50th percentile. The middle group started at the 50th and stopped just before the 90th, where the top tenth began. These boundaries use sampling weights, so the lowest half of the weighted ranking need not contain half the sample.” Readers must infer that these percentiles rank citation counts, not disruption scores, and how ties at the boundaries are handled.
issues.fix: Within each publication year, we ranked works by how many different later publications cited them. Works below citation rank 50 went in the least-cited group. Those at rank 50 or higher but below 90 went in the middle group. Those at rank 90 or higher went in the top group. Tied counts received the same rank. We used sampling weights to set the groups, so the least-cited group need not contain half the sampled works.

issues.problem: “A work is more disruptive when later works cite it instead of citing it together with its references.” In Figure 3 this sounds like an either-or classification of each work, and it omits the reference-only citations that affect the score.
issues.fix: The disruption score compares the number of later works citing the sampled work alone with the number citing it alongside at least one reference. Later works citing only the references also count toward the total used to scale the score. The plotted rank compares that score with scores for eligible works from the same year.

issues.problem: “The decline is clear in the least-cited half; the middle and top estimates and the contrast are uncertain.” The figure caption does not say here what “the contrast” compares or what readers should use to assess it.
issues.fix: The fitted decline is clear for the least-cited half, but not for the middle group or the top tenth. The direct comparison below tests whether disruption rank fell faster in the top tenth than in the least-cited half. The bars on the plotted averages do not answer that question.

issues.problem: “In a direct comparison the estimated change per doubling was 2.73 points higher in the top tenth than in the bottom half. The 95% interval ran from 1.89 points lower to 6.00 points higher, across 3,734 works.” After several negative changes, “higher” makes readers work out whether it means a steeper decline or a weaker one.
issues.fix: For each doubling of team size, the change in disruption rank was 2.73 points more positive in the top tenth than in the least-cited half. In other words, the best estimate points toward a weaker decline at the top. The 95% interval ran from 1.89 points more negative to 6.00 points more positive. The comparison used 3,734 works, and the interval allows either group to have the steeper decline.

issues.problem: “OpenAlex’s main topic places each classified work in a broad subject and a narrower subject within it. We used these subjects for the field and subfield comparisons.” “Main topic” sounds like a system label rather than an explanation of how the groups were assigned.
issues.fix: For each work that OpenAlex classified by subject, we used its primary subject classification. We call the broad subject a field and the narrower subject within it a subfield.

issues.problem: “Fourteen of 20 fields had a negative estimate: 70%, with a 95% interval of 55% to 80%, across 6,074 works. So did 24 of 34 subfields: 71%, with an interval of 53% to 76%, across 3,601 works.” The percentages count fields or subfields, but the adjoining work counts can make them look like percentages of works. A “negative estimate” also need not be a clear decline for an individual field.
issues.fix: The best estimate pointed to a decline in 14 of 20 fields, or 70%. The 95% interval for that percentage was 55% to 80%. Those fields contained 6,074 works. For subfields, 24 of 34 pointed to a decline, or 71%, with a 95% interval of 53% to 76%. Those subfields contained 3,601 works. These counts include groups whose individual intervals still allowed no change or a rise.

issues.problem: “The dots show the estimated difference in disruption rank across works for a doubling of the number of authors. The dashed line marks no estimated difference.” The caption does not tell readers which side of the line means a decline. It also sends them to “the second table column” rather than naming what the column shows.
issues.fix: Each dot shows the estimated change in disruption rank for a doubling of team size in one field. Values below zero mean that larger teams ranked lower. The dashed line marks zero change. The table reports how many fields, subfields and journals met the sample requirements out of all those represented in the sample.

issues.problem: “The original study reported both patterns and proposed models for how older references and very highly cited references become rarer. The direct comparison of reference lists is separate from those model checks.” The reader does not yet know which quantities the models describe or how those checks differ from the observed comparison.
issues.fix: First we compared the recorded reference lists: how old their sources were and how often those sources had been cited. Separately, we tested whether simple mathematical descriptions matched how the share of references falls as the age cutoff or the citation-count cutoff rises.

issues.problem: “Longer lists therefore contribute more. In a separate comparison, we calculated the average age of each work’s references first, so a long list did not give that work more influence.” The second comparison could sound unweighted, even though the point is to remove extra influence from list length, not from sampling.
issues.fix: In the figure, each listed reference gets the sampling weight of the work that lists it, so longer lists contribute more. In the separate comparison, we first calculated one average reference age per work and then compared those averages using the works’ sampling weights. A longer list did not give the work extra influence in that comparison.

issues.problem: “In order of 1, 10 and 51–100 authors, both panels use 597, 624 and 477 works. Panel A uses 22,001, 34,531 and 43,548 links; panel B uses 22,149, 34,613 and 43,772.” Readers have to match several lists of numbers and infer what counts as a “link.”
issues.fix: Both panels show 597 solo works, 624 works by 10 authors, and 477 works by 51 to 100 authors. A reference counts once for each work that lists it. For solo works, panel A counts 22,001 references this way and panel B counts 22,149. For works by 10 authors, the counts are 34,531 and 34,613. For works by 51 to 100 authors, they are 43,548 and 43,772.

issues.problem: “Panel B uses current citation totals, not totals at publication. Its scale is linear through one citation and logarithmic above one.” “At publication” could mean the publication of the source or of the work citing it. The explanation of “logarithmic” appears outside the caption.
issues.fix: Panel B uses the totals recorded when we collected the data, not the totals when the work listing each reference was published. On the horizontal axis, spacing is even up to one citation. Above one citation, equal distances represent a tenfold increase in the count. Put this explanation in the caption rather than repeating it below the figure.

issues.problem: “The model comparison among references with at least 50 citations was inconclusive.” The Figure 5 caption does not say which teams were compared or what the evidence could not establish. It also puts the separate model results into a caption for curves that do not show the models.
issues.fix: In the caption, say that the curves show the recorded data and do not show a fitted model. In the results text, say: Among references with at least 50 citations, we could not tell whether higher citation counts became rarer at different rates for ten-author and solo works.

issues.problem: “Neither model fit closely: in the ten-author group, the fitted and observed shares at or below a cutoff differed by as much as 8.1 percentage points for age, using 34,531 reference records from 624 works, and 8.8 points for citations in the fitted range, using 26,259 records from 620 works.” This packs two results, four sample counts and an undefined comparison into one sentence.
issues.fix: Neither model matched the data closely for ten-author works. We compared the share of references at or below each cutoff with the share predicted by the model. The largest gap for reference age was 8.1 percentage points, based on 34,531 listed references from 624 works. For citation counts in the range covered by the model, the largest gap was 8.8 points, based on 26,259 listed references from 620 works.

issues.problem: “In the second, we counted citations from publication through the end of the second full calendar year and asked what share arrived in the publication year itself. For this comparison we gave the groups the same mix of publication years and three-month periods within each year.” It is unclear how the groups were made comparable, how each work’s share entered the result, or which publication years had enough follow-up.
issues.fix: The second measure asks what share of a work’s citations arrived in its publication year, out of all citations it received through the end of the second full calendar year after publication. We compared the groups as if the same share of their works had been published in each year and each three-month period. State how those shares were made comparable, which works needed at least one citation, and which publication years had enough follow-up for each measure.

issues.problem: “The first full year accounted for 5.23 percentage points more of the early citation total for teams with 51 to 100 authors than for solo works.” This sounds like citations were pooled across each group, rather than that the analysis averaged shares calculated separately for each work.
issues.fix: For each work, we calculated the share of citations in the first of the two full calendar years after publication. The weighted average of that share was 5.23 percentage points higher for teams with 51 to 100 authors than for solo works.

issues.problem: “Works with negative scores had a greater publication-year share than works with positive scores, by 2.14 percentage points. The 95% interval was 1.04 to 3.19 points, across 5,421 works. The difference was unclear using the two full years instead.” Both share measures use the two full years in some way; the last sentence does not identify the alternative.
issues.fix: Works with negative scores received 2.14 percentage points more of their early citations in the publication year than works with positive scores. The 95% interval was 1.04 to 3.19 points, based on 5,421 works. We could not establish a difference when we looked only at the next two full calendar years and asked what share arrived in the first of those years.

issues.problem: “We used works with one to ten authors by people whom OpenAlex identified and linked to Columbia and who appeared on eligible works with different numbers of authors. We fitted a trend that lets each author, year and topic have a different average rank, rather than counting those differences as part of the team-size pattern.” It is hard to tell exactly which authors qualified, what “topic” means here, and what the trend compares.
issues.fix: We used works with one to ten authors. An author qualified if OpenAlex identified the person, recorded the required Columbia affiliation, and listed the person on eligible works with different team sizes. State where the affiliation had to be recorded and which OpenAlex subject category was used. We compared team sizes among works by the same authors while allowing average ranks to differ by publication year and subject.

issues.problem: “The adjusted decline was 1.85 rank points per doubling, with a 95% interval of 0.27 to 3.43 points, across 4,107 works. Without adjustment on those same works, the decline was 1.73 points, with an interval of 0.46 to 3.01.” “Adjusted” is shorthand for the previous paragraph, and the second estimate drops the unit and direction from its interval.
issues.fix: After allowing for differences by author, year and topic, each doubling of team size was associated with a decline of 1.85 rank points. The 95% interval was a decline of 0.27 to 3.43 points. For the same 4,107 works, the estimate without allowing for those differences was a decline of 1.73 points per doubling, with a 95% interval of 0.46 to 3.01 points of decline.

issues.problem: “Work that OpenAlex classified as articles ranked lower as team size increased. For work classified as reviews, the evidence did not establish a decline.” A review can also be an article in everyday usage, so the comparison can look like one between overlapping groups.
issues.fix: We compared works that OpenAlex labeled as articles with works it labeled separately as reviews. Larger teams ranked lower among works labeled as articles. For works labeled as reviews, the evidence did not establish a decline.

issues.problem: “Across 4,405 works with one to ten authors, a doubling of team size corresponded to a fall of 3.01 rank points in the main window and 2.82 in the shorter window. The 95% intervals were declines of 2.01 to 3.93 and 1.78 to 3.85 points, respectively. The interval on the difference between the changes included zero.” The reader has to match two intervals to two estimates and translate the last sentence into the conclusion about follow-up.
issues.fix: We compared the same 4,405 works with one to ten authors. In the main period, the estimated decline was 3.01 rank points per doubling, with a 95% interval of 2.01 to 3.93 points of decline. In the shorter period, the decline was 2.82 points, with a 95% interval of 1.78 to 3.85 points of decline. The direct comparison did not establish that the decline differed between the two periods.

issues.problem: “The team-size pattern differed depending on whether the index listed a funding acknowledgment.” “Depending on” suggests that funding, or its recording, explains the difference.
issues.fix: The estimated link between team size and disruption rank differed between works with and without a funding acknowledgment recorded in OpenAlex.

issues.problem: “The rate at which older references became rarer and the shape of the highest citation counts differed by team size.” In the summary table, “shape of the highest citation counts” is not a result a reader can interpret without going back to the model section.
issues.fix: The original study reported that team size was related to how quickly older references became less common and how quickly references became less common as their citation counts rose.

issues.problem: “Funding acknowledgment records allow only a local description. The historical, company patent and prize samples are absent.” “Local description” and “samples are absent” make the summary table less direct than the main text.
issues.fix: This Columbia sample lets us compare works with and without a funding acknowledgment in OpenAlex, but not works known to be funded or unfunded. It does not contain the data needed for comparisons over decades, for company patents, or for work associated with Nobel Prizes.

issues.problem: “Ranking works within a publication year avoids comparing ranks directly across years with different amounts of time to collect citations.” The analyses do use ranks from different years together. What is avoided when calculating those ranks is a direct comparison of scores from different years.
issues.fix: We first ranked each work’s score against those of eligible works from the same publication year. We then used those within-year ranks in the team-size comparisons. This avoids ranking scores from different publication years against each other, but earlier works within a year still had more time to be cited.

issues.problem: “The cutoff uses publication dates; it does not tell us what records the index contained on that date. The count checks show that the available records were counted consistently in the cases checked, not that every citation was recorded.” The distinction between the cutoff and the copy of the index is important but abstract.
issues.fix: We used 23 November 2026 to decide which publication dates to count. We did not reconstruct what OpenAlex contained on that date. Our checks show that the counting methods agreed for the records we tested. They do not show that OpenAlex had recorded every citation.

issues.problem: “The intervals do not account for index errors, the same later publication affecting the scores of several works, or differences at other universities.” Three different limitations are compressed into one list, and the middle one does not explain how the results are linked.
issues.fix: A single later publication can contribute to several sampled works’ scores. The intervals do not allow for that link between scores or for errors in OpenAlex. They also do not show how much the findings might differ at other universities.

issues.problem: “We excluded 10,720 for which the index listed no reference links and reported a reference count of zero. The rule also barred any record with a positive count but no usable link. We excluded another 4,110 works with references but no evidence of being cited, leaving 40,541 works on the sampling list.” The totals reconcile only if the second sentence adds no further exclusions, but the passage does not say that.
issues.fix: Of 55,371 Columbia-linked works, 10,720 had no usable reference links and a recorded reference count of zero. The rule also rejected a positive reference count without a usable link. State explicitly whether any records met that condition and where they are counted. Another 4,110 works had usable references but lacked evidence of a citation. The sampling list contained 40,541 works.

issues.problem: “The draw used records sorted by their OpenAlex identifiers and the PCG64 random-number method with 42 as its starting value.” The software detail interrupts the explanation of selection, and “identifiers” and “starting value” could be clearer.
issues.fix: Explain the sampling rule first: we randomly selected works within each team-size group without selecting any work twice. Then give the reproducibility detail separately: to make the draw repeatable, we sorted the records by their OpenAlex record numbers and used the PCG64 random-number generator with the starting value 42.

issues.problem: “In the main window, 7,933 works were cited, 64 had only their references cited and three had neither cited. In the shorter window, 6,012 works had complete follow-up. Of those, 5,671 were cited, 339 had only their references cited and two had neither cited.” “Neither cited” has to be decoded, and “complete follow-up” can be mistaken for a guarantee that the database recorded every citation.
issues.fix: By the main cutoff, 7,933 sampled works had been cited themselves. For 64, at least one reference was cited but the work itself was not. For three, neither the work nor any of its references was cited in the index. The shorter period had ended for 6,012 sampled works. Of those, 5,671 were themselves cited in that period, 339 had citations only to their references, and two had citations to neither the work nor its references.

issues.problem: “For long lists, a later work could cite references in several parts of the list. We counted it only in the first part it matched. Lists retrieved directly were checked against expected counts and duplicate identifiers were removed when combining lists.” The reader has not been told why there are parts, what was retrieved directly, or where the expected counts came from.
