issues.fix: When we searched a long reference list in separate batches, the same later publication could match references in more than one batch. We counted it only in the first batch where it appeared. When we combined lists of citing publications, we removed repeated records. Name the lists obtained directly and explain what independent count or reported total each list was checked against.

issues.problem: “In all 62 checks, totals from grouping records matched totals calculated separately. In one separate check of a later part of a long list, all 122 citing works checked cited a reference in that part and none in an earlier part. In seven checks for individual works and years, reversing the order of the parts did not change the totals. Each of the 79 lists retrieved directly contained the expected number of distinct citing works.” The figures are specific but the checks are not: “grouping,” “separately,” and “expected” do not identify the comparisons.
issues.fix: Start with the point: the checks tested whether the counting methods agreed, not whether OpenAlex was complete. For the 62 comparisons, name the two ways of obtaining the same total. In one batch check, all 122 later publications cited a reference in that batch and none cited a reference in an earlier batch. In seven checks for particular works and years, reversing the batches left the counts unchanged. Each of the 79 lists contained the expected number of distinct citing publications; identify where that expected number came from.

issues.problem: “The bootstrap used 1,000 repeat draws with random-number seed 20261123. Each repeat drew the original number of works from each group, allowing repeats, then reapplied eligibility rules and recalculated ranks and citation groups.” It is easy to mistake a repeat draw for a draw from only the final set of eligible works. The significance of treating the fully sampled largest group the same way is explained only afterward.
issues.fix: We made 1,000 new draws from the original sample, not just from the works that qualified for analysis. Each draw kept the original number of works in each team-size group and could pick a work more than once. We then checked eligibility again and recalculated the ranks and citation groups. We did this even for the largest group, where the original sample contained all 481 listed works. The starting value 20261123 lets others repeat the draws.

issues.problem: “The regression intervals hold the ranks fixed and use two-way clustering, which lets records sharing an author or a work be related when estimating the uncertainty. The appendix table also shows a separate bootstrap interval for the unadjusted trend, which does recalculate ranks.” The technical wording makes it hard to see what changes between the two intervals and what stays the same.
issues.fix: For the comparisons by author, we used the ranks already calculated. We allowed records to be related if they shared either an author or a work. This is called two-way clustering. For the trend that does not account for year, topic or author, the table also gives an interval from repeated draws. Those draws recalculate ranks but do not change which trend the row reports.

issues.problem: “Counting a reference once per work that listed it gave 446,323 records covering 373,977 different references.” The distinction is important in the tables, but “records” is used for several different things in the report.
issues.fix: The same source can appear on several reference lists. Counting it once for each work that listed it gave 446,323 appearances of 373,977 different sources. In the reference tables, use “listed references” for appearances and “distinct sources” when each source is counted only once.

issues.problem: “As an illustration, one citation becomes one and three become two. This reduces the influence of very highly cited references. A difference in the table is a difference between averages on that scale, not a difference in numbers of citations.” The examples skip the add-one step, and the tables call this merely an “adjusted scale,” which is easy to confuse with the adjustment for year, topic and author.
issues.fix: Name this the logarithmic citation scale in the table. For one citation, adding one gives two, which is one doubling from one. Its value on the scale is one. For three citations, adding one gives four, which is two doublings from one. Its value is two. The table compares averages on this scale, not average numbers of citations.

issues.problem: “The fitted age parameter is the negative natural logarithm of the fraction still above the cutoff with each additional year. The fitted citation parameter is the exponent in a power law: doubling a citation count multiplies the model frequency by one divided by two raised to that exponent.” Both definitions lead with technical operations before saying what the resulting numbers measure. “Model frequency” is also undefined.
issues.fix: Start with the interpretation: the age number measures how quickly older references become less common. If nine tenths of the share remains after an extra year, that number is smaller than if eight tenths remains. Then give the exact conversion once: take the natural logarithm of the fraction remaining and reverse its sign. For references with at least 50 citations, the citation number measures how quickly the predicted frequency of a citation count falls as the count rises. It is the exponent in a power law: when the count doubles, an exponent of one leaves half the predicted frequency and an exponent of two leaves one quarter. In both rows, explain that a positive difference means a faster fitted drop for ten-author than for solo works.

issues.problem: “We compared modeled and observed shares at or below each cutoff to describe fit, not to test it as if individual reference records were independent.” The reader is left to infer why references cannot be treated as independent and whether the fit check was a formal test.
issues.fix: We compared the share the model predicted at or below each cutoff with the share we observed. We used the gaps to describe how closely the model matched the data, not as a formal test. Several references can come from the same work, and several works can list the same reference.

issues.problem: “The first results column requires a citation to the work itself. The second also admits a work if only its references were cited.” The repeated header “Works cited” can be mistaken for a count or for an instruction about which citations go into the disruption score, rather than about which sampled works are included.
issues.fix: Label the columns “Only works themselves cited” and “Also includes works whose references alone were cited.” Explain that the columns change which sampled works are included, not how the main disruption score counts later publications. In the reference table, label the last column “Sampled works regardless of whether they were cited.”

issues.problem: “A gap of 0.294 on a share scale is 29.4 percentage points. That happens to be close to the estimated difference in the shares scoring below zero, but it is a different calculation.” The reported figures are the same at the displayed precision, so “close” distracts from the actual distinction.
issues.fix: The largest gap anywhere on the score scale was 0.294, or 29.4 percentage points. At the precision shown, that is also the difference between the shares scoring below zero. The first calculation looks for the largest gap at any cutoff. The second compares the groups only just below zero.

issues.problem: “Difference in fitted exponent for highly cited references” and “Difference in citations, counting every listed reference (adjusted scale)” are difficult to interpret as table labels, even after the methods explanation.
issues.fix: Use “Difference in how quickly higher citation counts become rarer, for references with at least 50 citations” and “Difference in average citations on the logarithmic scale, counting each listed reference.” Keep the exact unit and model term in a short note beneath the table.

issues.problem: “Change per doubling: main window, years with complete short follow-up” and “Change per doubling: main window, using only works eligible in both windows” look nearly interchangeable, but the rows deliberately use different sets of works.
issues.fix: Use “Main-period change in rank per doubling, for works published early enough to measure both periods” and “Main-period change in rank per doubling, for works that met the citation rule in both periods.” Note that the first set can include works cited only after the shorter period ended.

issues.problem: “62.46 (59.99 to 64.78); 600” illustrates how the appendix makes readers decode the estimate, interval and sample count in one cell while displaying more digits than are needed to see the result.
issues.fix: Keep 62.46, 59.99 and 64.78 in the cited evidence. For a reader-facing table, show the average rank and its 95% interval to three significant digits: 62.5, with an interval of 60.0 to 64.8. Keep the sample count of 600 exact and label it separately.
